messages.subject: Non-structured component variance (sigma^2 eps)
parts:
Hello all, 

I'm having trouble figuring the variance of my non-spatial, non-temporal components in my model. I'm using a variation of the code used in Musenge et al. 2013, Bayesian analysis of zero inflated spatiotemporal HIV/TB child mortality data through the INLA and SPDE approaches: Applied to data observed between 1992 and 2010 in rural North East South Africa. 

They do their temporal aspect a little differently than the Cameletti 2012 example, simply specifying the AR1 as another random effect rather than using the "Group" functionality to include it in the SPDE. (Is this still correct?)

Here is an example of my code:

loc<-cbind(DataWithDaymet$Long,DataWithDaymet$Lat) #Stores the lat/longs of each observation site
bnd<-inla.nonconvex.hull(loc,convex=0.1) #Makes a nonconvex hull around the points rather than the spatial extent of the island
mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bnd, cutoff=0.05, max.edge=c(0.1,0.2))

#Creating the INLA with 1 week weather lag
A <-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc)
spde<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh,alpha=2)
formula<-Result ~ -1 + SepCt + NDVI + OpWat + DevLow + WWet+ EHWet + PrcpL1 + TavgL1 + f(spatial, model=spde) + f(Week, model= "ar1")
vars<-DataWithDaymet[,c(5,7,8,9,10,15,16,32,39)] #Week is included here, in Vars
vars[,(1:9)]<- sapply(vars[,(1:9)],as.numeric)
vars[,2:9]<-scale(vars)[,2:9] #Scaling by mean and SD
stk<-inla.stack(data=list(Result=DataWithDaymet$Result),A=list(A,1),effect=list(list(spatial=1:spde$n.spde),data.frame(vars)))
r<-inla(formula, family="zeroinflatedbinomial1", control.family=list(link="logit"), data=inla.stack.data(stk), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk)),control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))
summary(r)

and here is an example of the output:



I can see how to calculate tau and kappa from the thetas, and how to use those to obtain sigma^2 for the spatial component. However, I don't see the "Precision for the Gaussian observations" that is used in the Cameletti paper to obtain the variance. Am I doing something wrong? 



Thanks very much, 


Mark Myer

On 22 Sep 2016, at 15:25, Mark Myer <thereal...@gmail.com> wrote:
I'm having trouble figuring the variance of my non-spatial, non-temporal components in my model. I'm using a variation of the code used in Musenge et al. 2013, Bayesian analysis of zero inflated spatiotemporal HIV/TB child mortality data through the INLA and SPDE approaches: Applied to data observed between 1992 and 2010 in rural North East South Africa. 

They do their temporal aspect a little differently than the Cameletti 2012 example, simply specifying the AR1 as another random effect rather than using the "Group" functionality to include it in the SPDE. (Is this still correct?)

They are both valid models. In Cameletti, the covariance is the product
of a spatial and a temporal covariance function. In Musenge, it's the sum
of the covariances instead of the product, which is more restrictive in terms
of what kind of behaviour the combined model can exhibit.
Here is an example of my code:

I can see how to calculate tau and kappa from the thetas, and how to use those to obtain sigma^2 for the spatial component. However, I don't see the "Precision for the Gaussian observations" that is used in the Cameletti paper to obtain the variance. Am I doing something wrong?

You're using a zero inflated binomial model, which has a different parameter
 than the Gaussian observation likelihood used in Cameletti.  Which variance are 
you looking for here?

For the spde parameters tau and kappa I would suggest using the inla.spde.result()
function to extract the parameter estimates for the spde model, since that will help
with the conversion to interpretable values. (Log range and log variance).
At least as a double check that your own conversion is correct.

Finn

Thanks very much, 


Mark Myer

Finn, 

OK, I think I see my mistake. I thought that the "zero-probability parameter" was something else. I'm looking for the variance in the final model not explained by either the spatial or temporal component, so that I can make some comparison ("the spatial and temporal components explained x amount of the total variance, while the non-spatiotemporal error of the model was y"). 

Basically, something analogous to this section of the Cameletti paper for the zero inflated Binomial, I'm looking for the σ^2 ε :

 \We note that the inla(.) function provides us with the mean, quantiles and standard deviation of the Gaussian observation precision parameter 1/σ2 ε . As we are interested in the variance σ 2 ε , we need to transform the marginal density of the precision using the inla.tmarginal(.) function, as  \follows sigma2eps_marg = inla.tmarginal(function(x) 1/x, result$marginals.hyperpar$"Precision for the Gaussian observations") Then using the inla.emarginal(.) and inla.eqmarginal(.) functions we can easily compute the mean, the standard deviation and the quantiles of σ 2 ε , given in Table 3:

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Non-structured component variance (sigma^2 eps)
parts:
Hi Mark,
I see what you're asking, but I'm not sure if it's an entirely well-posed question, since the  linear model part (spatial and covariate contributions) has a non-linear link to the observation model (the zero-inflated binomial). Therefore the "variance explained" by the two parts of the model are not additive (or even in the same scale!).

Perhaps you could go another route, and look at the difference in predictive precision between the full model and that of a simple model (e.g. one with just an intercept).  But there might be people in the email group with better ideas.

Finn
